title: Measure and draw angles with a protractor

lesson.title: Using a Protractor: Read the Right Number!

steps.say: You already know that a right angle is ninety degrees and a straight line is one hundred eighty degrees, so you can guess if an angle is bigger or smaller than those. Today we learn how to get the exact number using a protractor, the way you would measure your height in centimetres instead of just saying 'tall'.

visual.caption: You already know this one: a right angle, ninety degrees

steps.say: Here are the three steps. Step one, put the little hole or cross in the middle of the protractor right on the corner point of the angle. Step two, turn the protractor so one arm lies flat along the zero line. Step three, follow the other arm out to the edge and read the number. Each step matters: the hole makes the angle open from the centre, and the zero line makes your counting start at zero, just like starting a ruler at zero centimetres and not at three.

visual.caption: Centre on the corner, one arm on zero, read where the other arm points

steps.say: Let's measure a real one. Imagine the hands of the clock on the wall of your classroom making this angle. You line up the bottom arm on zero. The other arm crosses the edge at two numbers printed there: sixty and one hundred twenty. Which one is right? Look back at where your arm started. It started at zero, and sixty comes from that same zero, so this angle is sixty degrees.

visual.caption: Started at zero, so we read sixty degrees

steps.say: Here is the mistake almost everybody makes. Someone reads that same angle as one hundred twenty degrees, because they grabbed the number from the other scale. But think about it with your estimating eyes. This angle is clearly smaller than a square corner, smaller than ninety degrees. One hundred twenty is bigger than ninety, so it cannot be right. The trick is simple: if your arm started at zero on the inside scale, read the inside scale the whole way. Never jump from one scale to the other.

visual.caption: This is what one hundred twenty degrees really looks like — much wider than our angle

steps.say: Drawing an angle is the same three steps backwards. Say you want to draw one hundred thirty five degrees. Draw a straight arm first, put the protractor centre on its end, line the arm up with zero, count up the scale that starts at zero until you reach one hundred thirty five, make a tiny dot there, then join the dot to the corner. Check with your eyes: it is wider than a square corner but not a straight line, so one hundred thirty five feels just right.

visual.caption: One hundred thirty five degrees: wider than a corner, not yet a straight line

steps.say: So before you write your answer down, always give it the eyeball test. Smaller than a square corner means the number must be under ninety. Bigger means over ninety. That one quick check saves you from the wrong scale every single time.

lesson.answer: Start at zero and stay on that same scale — then check: under a square corner means under ninety degrees.

practice.question: On a ski hill sign at Grouse Mountain, a ramp arm goes up from a flat line. You measure it with your protractor and the arm lands where two numbers are printed: forty and one hundred forty. The ramp angle looks much smaller than a square corner. Which number is the correct measurement, and how do you know?
practice.answer: Forty degrees. The angle looks smaller than a square corner, and a square corner is ninety degrees, so the answer must be under ninety. One hundred forty is from the other scale — the one that does not start at zero where your arm started.
